newsitem.title: USA: Clinton consults world leaders on Zaire crisis.
newsitem.headline: Clinton consults world leaders on Zaire crisis.

text.p: President Bill Clinton discussed Zaire's refugee crisis with other world leaders by telephone on Wednesday amid signs he was close to approving U.S. military involvement in a relief operation.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry said among those Clinton expected to consult was Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien, whose government offered to lead a multinational force to the region.
The mission of the proposed force would be to aid starving refugees in eastern Zaire who have been fleeing fighting between Tutsi rebels and Zaire's army.

In Rome, U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman said the United States was ready to provide humanitarian aid and support to refugees in Africa's Great Lakes region as soon as the right mechanisms could be established.

Glickman made the announcement at the World Food Summit without spelling out whether such support would be in the form of participation in a multinational force being organised to confront the crisis in eastern Zaire.

McCurry said before committing U.S. troops Clinton wanted to reconcile "different objectives and different ideas presented by different nations" and seek the support of African countries whose interests might be affected.

"Even facing an urgent humanitarian situation, there always is a necessity for the commander-in-chief to have a very clear focus on mission priorities, objectives, who participates, how the force would be structured, what the nature and the duration of the mission would be and how do you measure success and how do you get out," McCurry said.
The United States has painful memories of a U.N. relief mission to Somalia in 1993 which led to heavy casualties among U.S. and other troops.

Most of the refugees in eastern Zaire are Hutus who fled Rwanda in 1994 when rebels of the Tutsi minority ousted the Hutu-dominated government that had orchestrated the genocide of hundreds of thousands of Tutsis and moderate Hutus.

A military-led U.S. assessment team has been sent to the region. The team, headed by U.S. Army Maj. Gen. Edward Smith, commander of the South European Task Force based in Vicenza, Italy, arrived in Central Africa earlier on Wednesday.
Sources at the United Nations said the United States was expected to offer troops, although less than some expected, and join the operation.

Clinton appeared certain to approve the operation under Canadian leadership and its proposed commander, Lt. Gen. Maurice Baril, head of Canada's land forces and the former chief military adviser at the United Nations, they said.

The sources said Britain also was expected to announce its participation, clearing the way for the Security Council to get to work on a resolution, which Canada drafted, that could be adopted before the end of the week.
